name: Mbaŋwɛ
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Koumbi Mabiti, Glenn Aymar. 2025. Phonologie diachronique des parlers du groupe Kota-Kele (B20) pour un affinement des embranchements internes. PhD thesis, Université Omar Bongo, Libreville. 382 pp. HAL tel-04957912 (open access). The synchronic Mbaŋwɛ phonology in §I.2.2.2 is explicitly taken over from Mokrani, Soraya. 2016. catalog_locator: §I.2.2.2.1.3 'Système tonal', p. 69; §I.2.2.2.2.3 'Organisation des tonèmes', p. 72; B20-wide remark in the 'Observations globales' at the end of §II.1.2.4 'Le schème *BH' (within §II.1.2 'Analyses supra segmentales', just before the mis-numbered heading 'I.1.3 Analyses des structures syllabiques'), p. 238.
catalog_quote: I.2.2.2.1.3 Système tonal L’inventaire des réalisations tonales laissent entrevoir un système simple composé de deux tons simples et de deux tons modulés. - Ton Haut noté (H) - Ton Bas noté (B) - Ton Montant noté (Mt) et - Ton Descendant noté (Dt) [p. 69] ... I.2.2.2.2.3 Organisation des tonèmes Sur le plan tonal, l’opération de commutation a permis de relever que le mbaŋwɛ manifeste deux (2) tonèmes, à savoir: un tonème /H/et un tonème /B/ respectivement représenté par / ʹ/ et / ˋ/. Les tons ont une fonction distinctive dans la langue. L’auteur relève un ton moyen qui serait la réalisation d’un ton haut devant pause. Un ton Haut Abaissés (HA) qui résulterait de la succession de deux ton haut (haut-haut). [p. 72] ... La quasi-absence d’opposition tonale H/B amorcée en T2, vient du fait que la syllabe finale des thèmes est régulièrement réalisée avec un ton bas. Tels qu’observés, les faits pourraient conforter comme l’ont suggéré, J, P. Rekanga (2007. p. 26) et E. Dodo-Bouguendza (2010. p. 78) une évolution vers un processus accentuel. Diachroniquement, la situation laisse entrevoir un processus évolutif amorcé et non encore achevé puisque l’on peut également observer des tons haut en position T2, bien que faiblement représenté. [p. 238, on the B20 group as a whole]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.translation: On the tonal level, the commutation test showed that Mbaŋwɛ has two tonemes, a high toneme /H/ and a low toneme /B/, written / ʹ/ and / ˋ/. Tones have a distinctive function in the language. The author [Mokrani 2016] notes a mid tone which would be the realisation of a high tone before pause, and a downstepped high (HA) which would result from a sequence of two high tones (high-high). [p. 72] ... As observed, the facts could support, as J.-P. Rekanga (2007: 26) and E. Dodo-Bouguendza (2010: 78) have suggested, an evolution towards an accentual process. [p. 238, about the B20 group]

Un ton Haut Abaissés (HA) qui résulterait de la succession de deux ton haut (haut-haut)." -- verbatim as reported (only a line break inside "haut-haut" differs). p. 239 = printed "Page | 238": "Tels qu'observés, les faits pourraie…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mbangwe is described as a two-toneme (H/L) tone language with distinctive tone; the source says nothing about word stress for Mbangwe. The only accent-related remark is diachronic and group-wide: across the 14 B20 varieties studied (Mbaŋwɛ included) the H/L contrast is being lost on the second stem syllable (T2, regularly low), which the author reads as possibly the start of an accentual system, not as an existing stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Mbangwe; the p. 238 remark notes the process is 'begun and not yet complete' since some H tones remain in T2.
new_statements.domain_note: Nominal and verbal stems (disyllabic stem T1/T2 positions) in citation form, from a 413-item comparative wordlist; the tonal description of Mbangwe is a summary of Mokrani 2016 ('L'auteur' = Mokrani), while the B20-wide tonal analysis of Part II is the author's own data (Mbaŋwɛ informant Matangoye Serge, Franceville, listed in the annex).
new_statements.identity_note: Koumbi Mabiti 2025 and Mokrani 2016 describe the Gabonese Mbaŋwɛ of the Franceville area (Haut-Ogooué; informant from Franceville), i.e. mban1268 proper; Koumbi Mabiti notes the language is also spoken across the border in Congo-Brazzaville (Lékoumou). Ovono Ngui 2011 calls the language 'mbani B23', an alternate name for the same variety. No dialect split is described.

tone_statements.citation: Blanchon, Jean A. 1988. Tonalité des nominaux à thème dissyllabique dans le groupe bantou B 20. Pholia 3: 37-52. Lyon: Laboratoire de Phonétique et Linguistique Africaine, CRLS - Université Lumière Lyon 2.
tone_statements.quote: mbaŋwɛ *BB > B-HB màdyɛ́ɛ́lì "barbes" bànzɔ́ɔ́kì "éléphants" myɔ́ɔ́yì "ventres" *BH > B-BH màsùyí "cheveux" mànzìyá "chemins" mààlí "huile" lìkɔ̀ɔ̀ŋɔ́ "lance" bàŋààndú "crocodiles" *HB > B-HB mànyúúlù "corps" màtúúyù "poitrines" *HH > B-HB màtsíŋì "cous" màkáyà "feuilles" Théoriquement, màbɛ̀ɛ̀yɛ́ "seins" et bàmvúyá "pluies", tous deux réflexes de *HB, devraient être màbɛ́ɛ́yɛ̀ et bàmvúyà, tandis que bínáámà "cuisses", réflexe de *BB, devrait être bìnáámà.
tone_statements.translation: mbaŋwɛ *LL > L-HL màdyɛ́ɛ́lì "beards" bànzɔ́ɔ́kì "elephants" myɔ́ɔ́yì "bellies" *LH > L-LH màsùyí "hair" mànzìyá "paths" mààlí "oil" lìkɔ̀ɔ̀ŋɔ́ "spear" bàŋààndú "crocodiles" *HL > L-HL mànyúúlù "bodies" màtúúyù "chests" *HH > L-HL màtsíŋì "necks" màkáyà "leaves" Theoretically, màbɛ̀ɛ̀yɛ́ "breasts" and bàmvúyá "rains", both reflexes of *HL, should be màbɛ́ɛ́yɛ̀ and bàmvúyà, while bínáámà "thighs", reflex of *LL, should be bìnáámà.
tone_statements.locator: p. 43, section 'mbaŋwɛ'; grouping and location p. 49 + fn. 3; Tableau I p. 52
tone_statements.summary: Gives Mbaŋwɛ reflexes of Proto-Bantu noun tone classes (isolation forms, H/B values) from Jacquot 1983 data; groups it tonally with Ndasa sud; no inventory count, TBU or stress statement.

sources.note: Mbaŋwɛ (B23) section I.2.2.2 (pp. 67-72), synchronic part taken over from Mokrani 2016: two tonemes /H/ and /B/ with distinctive function, mid tone = H before pause, downstepped H from H-H; rising/falling as phonetic realisations. Nothing about stress/accent for Mbangwe. Group-level (14 B20 varieties incl. Mbaŋwɛ, author's own data) p. 238: H/B opposition tends to vanish on the second stem syllable (T2), which 'could support, as Rekanga (2007: 26) and Dodo-Bouguendza (2010: 78) suggested, an evolution towards an accentual process' -- a diachronic B20-wide remark, not a word-stress rule.
